title: BORISOV AND OTHERS v. BULGARIA
summary:
In Borisov and Others v. Bulgaria, the applicants were five Bulgarian nationals—Mr Boris Petkov Borisov, Mr Georgi Alexandrov Kirilov, Ms Iskra Borisova Mladenova, Mr Tassi Tsenov Tassev, and Mr Petko Borisov Traikov—along with the Roma Church in Bulgaria, an organisation they founded. All individual applicants identified as Roma, and their organisation aimed to serve the religious needs of the Roma community in Lom. The case centred on the vulnerability of Roma individuals seeking to exercise their religious freedom, facing repeated police interference and obstacles to official recognition of their religious group.

Between 1997 and 1999, the applicants’ religious gatherings in Lom were frequently disrupted by police, who warned them that unregistered religious activities were not permitted and ordered them to disperse. In 1998, Mr Borisov was detained for a week and questioned about his religious activities, and the prayer house they used was locked by police. After founding the Roma Church in Bulgaria in 1999, the applicants sought registration as a religious denomination, but their application was met with bureaucratic delays and requests for further information, ultimately leading to the Supreme Administrative Court rejecting their appeal as premature.

The European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under Articles 9 (freedom of religion), 11 (freedom of assembly), and 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court decided to adjourn examination of the complaints regarding disruption of religious meetings and registration, while declaring the remainder of the application inadmissible.

This case highlights the persistent barriers Roma and Traveller communities face in exercising religious and associational rights, reflecting broader patterns of marginalisation and the need for effective legal remedies in post-communist Europe.
